about: ARK-FISH (2026-11-23): the water animals that leave the water, and only those whose own stored text says so (production species_field_guide: species_spotlight, interesting_facts, signature_traits; read-only, quoted exactly). Rows: style, bouts per Ark day (mean), leaps per bout [min, max], the deciding quote, its field. Bouts and burst sizes are estimates from the quote's frequency words (often, regularly, several times in a row, long periods): flagged 'estimate'. Leaps that the text ties to a catch (an arowana's insect-catching leap, a great white's breach on prey, an orca's tail slaps on herring) or to being hooked (a mako) are left out: a leap here never implies a meal. Atlantic Salmon leaps only at a waterfall or weir (its text), and none is in its reach on the Ark today (it lives at sea), so it never leaps yet.

flathead-grey-mullet: Mullet often leap clear of the water, singly or in whole shoals, and the reason for this behaviour is still debated.
atlantic-tarpon: They are famous for dramatic leaps above the water.
indo-pacific-tarpon: Megalops cyprinoides is known for its shiny scales and incredible leaping ability.
thresher-shark: It can also leap clear of the water.
spotted-eagle-ray: it regularly launches itself clear of the surface, sometimes several times in a row.
tropical-two-wing-flyingfish: Swimming hard at the surface, it breaks out of the water and glides on stiff, outspread pectorals, commonly for tens of metres.
dusky-dolphin: Acrobatic leaps and twists above cold coastal water
spinner-dolphin: Spinner Dolphins can rotate multiple times in a single leap.
commersons-dolphin: it swims in fast, darting bursts, often turning and rolling at the surface.
southern-right-whale: Whales sometimes hold their flukes up in the wind for long periods, a behaviour watchers call sailing.
atlantic-salmon: At weirs and waterfalls, fish heading upstream hurl themselves clear of the water to climb the drop, trying again after each failure.
